summary: This article explains how the old covered souqs of historic Arab and Islamic cities were organized by craft, why they became the social and economic heart of the city, and how they differ from a modern mall.
introduce: Draw two overlapping circles on the board and quickly compare two familiar things, such as a cat and a dog, with the class. Tell students that while reading “Old Souqs: Markets of the Past” they will look for ways things are alike and different.

keyTerms.def: to talk back and forth with someone to agree on a price
cloth or fabric made by weaving or knitting threads
a group of people living and working at about the same time, such as parents or their children

challengeTerms.def: the buying and selling of goods, especially on a large scale
to argue or talk back and forth to agree on a lower price
the buildings, customs, and traditions passed down from the past

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that an old souq is a better place to shop than a modern mall? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain two ways a souq worked differently from a modern shopping mall.
struggling: Pre-teach bargain, textile, and generation with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use commerce, haggle, and heritage in a short paragraph that compares two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
